vignette:
She arrived for her appointment with her hands pressed flat against her thighs, her shoulders hunched forward as if bracing for impact. At nineteen, she looks younger—almost childlike in the way she shrinks into the armchair. She is married, she tells me, but the word comes out flat. Unemployed, she adds quickly, as though that needs explaining.

A year ago, she was walking home from a friend’s apartment when a man pulled her into an alley. It was late October, and she remembers the exact crunch of leaves under her attacker’s boots. He hit her once, then again, and the assault lasted long enough that she lost track of time. Afterward, she lay there until a woman found her and called an ambulance. She did not report it. The police asked, but she couldn’t form the words. She still can’t.

Three months later, she met her husband at a grocery store. He seemed steady, safe—a contrast to the chaos inside her. They married within six months. She thought marriage would be a kind of armor. It isn’t.

Now, she rarely leaves their one-bedroom apartment. Grocery shopping has become an ordeal: she scans every aisle for men with the same build, the same stride. A car backfiring on the street sends her to the floor. Her husband once touched her shoulder from behind to ask if she wanted coffee, and she screamed, then sobbed for an hour. He doesn’t touch her much anymore, and she doesn’t blame him.

Sleep is a minefield. She wakes three, sometimes four times a night, drenched in sweat, her heart pounding. The nightmare is always the same: the crunch of leaves, the weight of a body, the smell of damp concrete. She avoids television news, sidewalks, any mention of the word “alley.” She quit the community college she had been attending because the walk between buildings felt too exposed.

She tries to find work from home—data entry, survey sites—but concentration is impossible. Her mind wanders to the alley, or to the shame that sits like a stone in her chest. She believes she is ruined, that her husband would be better off without her. She checks her locks seven times before bed. She keeps a kitchen knife under her pillow. She knows it’s irrational, but the fear is louder than reason.

Her husband has stopped asking her to go out. He watches her from across the room. Sometimes he cries. She wants to comfort him, but she can’t find the words. She feels like a ghost in her own life—present, but not really there.

She says, “I used to want to be a teacher. Now I just want to feel safe in my own skin.”

She has not told anyone the full story. Not her mother, not her husband. The silence is another kind of weight. She carries it everywhere, even here, in this room, where she is finally speaking—but slowly, carefully, like someone testing ice.
